tip: 'Dol op' means crazy about: 'de kinderen zijn dol op chocolade'. The preposition is 'op'.
'Heimwee' (homesickness) is used with 'hebben' and 'naar': 'heimwee naar haar familie'.
Open with a time word and the verb still comes second, subject after it: 'gisteren kocht zij' (yesterday bought she).
'Geen ... meer' means not anymore: 'geen honger meer' is not hungry anymore.
'Nemen' (to take) is how you order or choose: 'wij nemen het driegangenmenu'.
Regular verbs form the past with '-de' or '-te': 'leven' becomes 'leefde' (lived).
'Te' before an adjective means too: 'te laat' is too late, 'te koud' is too cold.
'Als' means as for a role or job: 'een baan als monteur' (a job as a mechanic).
'Net' means just now and pairs with the perfect: 'ik ben net verhuisd' is I have just moved.
Most verbs form the perfect with 'hebben' plus a past participle at the end: 'ik heb je gemist' (I have missed you).
'Zich aanmelden' (to register) splits and keeps a self word: 'wij melden ons aan', with 'ons' after the verb and 'aan' at the end.
Separable 'uitleggen' splits apart in a main clause: 'de leraar legt de grammatica uit'.
'Inschenken' is separable; the prefix 'in' moves to the end: 'ik schenk koffie in' (I pour coffee).
'Jullie' is you in the plural; add 'allemaal' for you all: 'jullie allemaal'.
'Gaan' plus an infinitive expresses the near future, like English 'going to': 'ik ga boodschappen doen' (I'm going to shop).
'Broodje' is 'brood' plus '-je', a diminutive meaning a bread roll or sandwich.
'Heel' normally becomes 'hele' before a de-word: 'de hele familie' (the whole family).
'Helpen met' means to help with: 'hij helpt zijn buurman met de tuin'.
'Bekend om' means known for: 'de stad is bekend om haar grachten'. The preposition is 'om'.
The superlative usually adds '-ste' and uses 'van' for the group: 'de oudste van vier'.
'Al' with the present tense shows ongoing duration: 'ik woon al drie jaar' means I have lived here three years.
A de-word keeps the '-e' adjective even after 'een': 'een grote salade'.
Dutch 'half tien' means half to ten, so 9:30, not 10:30.
There is no word for of between container and content: 'een kop koffie' is a cup of coffee.
'Door' plus a noun can mean because of: 'door het slechte weer' is because of the bad weather.
Transport takes 'met': 'met de bus', 'met de trein', 'met de fiets' (by bus, train, bike).
Frequency is number + 'keer per' + time unit: 'twee keer per dag' = twice a day.
Means of transport takes 'met': 'met de auto' = by car.
'Stromend' is 'stromen' plus '-d', working like an adjective: 'stromend water' is running water.
A route uses 'van' for the origin and 'naar' for the destination: 'van Amsterdam naar Londen'.
